Measurements ▾

Choose a measurement, then click the atoms in the view. An angle takes three atoms, the vertex second. A dihedral takes four atoms in the order of the chain. An out-of-plane angle takes four: the bond runs from the first atom to the fourth, and the second, third and fourth make the plane. Dihedral and out-of-plane angle have the sign SLAPAF prints, so the numbers can be compared with its output. Atoms are numbered as in the file, from 1, ghost centres included, so a measurement keeps its atoms from frame to frame. Click a row to plot it; the plot uses the axis of the energy plot above (the path length along a path, the iteration otherwise). Measurements are drawn on the screen only, not in a recorded GIF.

Path ▾

The slider walks the converged path points, not the optimiser iterations between them. In an IRC the branch OpenMolcas computed first is called forward and the other backward; a minimum-energy path has one branch and no label. The path length is mass-weighted and measured along straight lines between the converged points, so it is slightly shorter than the cumulative length in the run output where the path bends. The file records the path points, not why a branch stopped; the run output says that.

Conical intersection ▾

g and h are the two directions that lift the degeneracy, taken from the last iteration. The arrows show one of them on the molecule, the longest 1 Å; the swing moves every atom along it, the largest by 0.3 Å (set the amplitude with the slider of the Vibrations section). The directions are plain Cartesian, not weighted by mass. The window has the numbers, the cones and the curves.

Convergence ▾

Click or tap a plot to show that iteration. The dashed line marks the restart of an IRC. Exports are drawn on white.

The amplitude is the largest displacement of any atom at the top of the swing. A mode is shown along the direction stored in the file, rescaled to that amplitude. Arrows show the direction of each atom's motion, the longest 1 Å; they could equally point the other way, since the sign of a mode is arbitrary (here the largest component is positive).

What is shown ▾

The last frame of a geometry file written by SLAPAF is not a computed geometry. SLAPAF writes one frame more than it computed: the geometry it has just worked out for the next iteration, with the energy it predicts for it and a force of zero because none was computed. The HDF5 file does not hold that frame. The tool recognises it by that zero force, marks it on the frame line, and draws its point in the energy plot as an open marker. The geometry file and the path file of an IRC (geo.molden and mep.molden) hold only the second branch; for the whole path open irc.molden or the HDF5 file.
